title: Separating Latent Allocation from Signal Recovery with Semi-Synthetic Positive Controls
content: A large shared latent block in a contrastive latent-variable model is often read as a shared biological response, but this reading is rarely tested against a known answer. We introduce a semi-synthetic positive-control benchmark that injects known 40-gene programs into measured mouse hippocampal control counts by binomial thinning, and use 315 fits of four latent-variable models and a direct differential-expression baseline to evaluate Multi-Condition Contrastive Variational Inference (MC-ContrastiveVI), which we also apply to cisplatin and doxorubicin hippocampal transcriptomes. On real data the model reconstructs held-out expression competitively (log-expression MSE 0.1686–0.1689) and allocates 92.4–97.0% of treatment-block posterior-mean variance to its shared block, yet no treatment coordinate is active and total shared divergence is 0.0109–0.0182 nats. Three results show that this shared fraction is uninformative about shared signal. Analytically, it is set by the latent dimension split: equal-scale collapsed blocks give 8/(8+4) = 0.67, and the split alone moves it from 0.22 to 0.93. Empirically, it does not separate 72 injected from 30 null fits (P = 0.11). Interventionally, flooring each dimension's Kullback–Leibler divergence raises utilization from 3.2 to 16 of 16 active coordinates and improves head-of-ranking recovery of the injected genes (median top-50 enrichment 1.13 to 2.25, P = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴), while the shared fraction falls (0.87 to 0.69) toward the value the split predicts. Global ordering never recovers, yet the direct baseline recovers the injected programs, so the signal is present in the data. Reconstruction, latent allocation and signal recovery are distinct criteria, and the benchmark offers a reusable test of a labeled latent block before it is interpreted biologically; code and per-fit results are released.
